topic: The Roots of Unity Filter: Using Complex Numbers in Combinatorial Counting
target_audience: Undergraduate students in mathematics or competitive programming enthusiasts

outline.topic: The Roots of Unity Filter: Using Complex Numbers in Combinatorial Counting
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate students in mathematics or competitive programming enthusiasts

sections.title: The Bridge: From Sequences to Polynomials
sections.content: Introduce the prerequisite concept of Generating Functions. Explain how a sequence of numbers (count of ways to do something) can be encoded as coefficients of a polynomial P(x). Use an animation showing a sequence of numbers 'flying' into the positions of coefficients in front of x^0, x^1, x^2...
sections.example: Suppose a 'Math Robot' can move 0, 1, or 2 steps. The ways to do this are encoded in P(x) = 1 + x + x^2.

sections.title: The Challenge: The Selective Sum
sections.content: Define the 'Filter' problem: We don't want the sum of all coefficients, but only every k-th coefficient (e.g., indices that are multiples of 3). Graphically, show a long polynomial where every 3rd term is highlighted while others dim out.
sections.example: If P(x) = a0 + a1x + a2x^2 + a3x^3..., how do we calculate the sum S = a0 + a3 + a6... efficiently?

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Magic of the Unit Circle
sections.content: Introduce Roots of Unity (ω). Use a complex plane visualization showing k points equally spaced on a unit circle. Demonstrate the 'Cancellation Property': the sum of these vectors is 0, unless they all align at 1 (when the power is a multiple of k).
sections.example: For k=3, show ω^0, ω^1, and ω^2 forming an equilateral triangle. Their vector sum is clearly (0,0).

sections.title: The Mechanism: The Filter Formula
sections.content: Combine the polynomial and the roots of unity. Present the formula: S = [P(ω^0) + P(ω^1) + ... + P(ω^{k-1})] / k. Explain how non-multiples of k 'spin' around the circle and cancel out, while multiples of k stay at the position (1,0) and add up.
sections.example: An animation showing terms spinning and collapsing into the center of the circle, leaving only the desired indices 'standing'.

sections.title: Application: Professor Penguin's Marble Problem
sections.content: Apply the theory to a concrete problem. Professor Penguin wants to choose a subset of N items such that the number of items chosen is a multiple of 3. We use the generating function P(x) = (1+x)^N.
sections.example: To find the sum of C(N, k) where k is a multiple of 3, we calculate [(1+1)^N + (1+ω)^N + (1+ω^2)^N] / 3 using the polar form of complex numbers.

sections.title: Summary and Conclusion
sections.content: Recap the workflow: 1. Build the Generating Function. 2. Identify the filter frequency (k). 3. Evaluate the polynomial at the k-th roots of unity. 4. Average the results. Emphasize that complex numbers turn a hard discrete counting problem into a simple continuous geometry problem.
sections.example: A final visual summary showing the transition: Sequence -> Polynomial -> Unit Circle -> Result.

storyboard.title: The Bridge: From Sequences to Polynomials
lecture_lines: Sequences can be encoded as polynomial coefficients.
We call this a Generating Function.
For a robot taking 0, 1, or 2 steps...
... we write P(x) = 1 + x + x^2.
Exponents track steps, coefficients track ways.
animations: Display sequence (1, 1, 1) in #FFFFFF at screen center.
Display P(x) = _ + _x + _x^2 template below the sequence.
Animate each '1' from the sequence moving into the blanks, turning them #FFFF00.

storyboard.title: The Challenge: The Selective Sum
lecture_lines: What if we only want specific terms?
Summing every third coefficient: a0, a3, a6...
This is the selective "Filter" problem.
animations: Display the polynomial P(x) = a0 + a1x + a2x^2 + a3x^3 + a4x^4 + a5x^5.
Change the color of coefficients a0 and a3 to #FFFF00 (Yellow).
Reduce opacity of all other terms (a1, a2, a4, a5) to 0.2.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Magic of the Unit Circle
lecture_lines: Meet the Roots of Unity on the unit circle.
For k=3, they form an equilateral triangle.
These vectors sum to zero, cancelling out.
But at x=1, they all align.
This cancellation property is our secret weapon.
animations: Draw a unit circle with Real and Imaginary axes labeled.
Plot three vectors (1, 0), (-0.5, 0.866), (-0.5, -0.866) in #00FFFF (Cyan).
Add labels ω^0, ω^1, and ω^2 next to the vector tips.
Animate the vectors moving tip-to-tail to form a closed equilateral triangle.
Fade the triangle and show the text 'Sum = 0' at the origin in #FFFF00.

storyboard.title: The Mechanism: The Filter Formula
lecture_lines: Evaluate the polynomial at each root of unity.
Summing these values isolates our desired terms.
Non-multiples spin around and vanish.
Multiples of k align and add up.
Dividing by k gives the selective sum.
animations: Display the filter formula S = 1/k * Σ P(ω^j) in #FFFFFF.
Expand the sum for k=3, showing P(ω^0) + P(ω^1) + P(ω^2).
Highlight the terms for coefficient a1: a1(1) + a1(ω^1) + a1(ω^2).
Animate the a1 terms spinning around the origin and cancelling to zero.
Highlight the a3 terms: a3(1) + a3(1) + a3(1) and show they sum to 3*a3.

storyboard.title: Application: Professor Penguin's Marble Problem
lecture_lines: Find subsets with size a multiple of 3.
Use the binomial expansion (1+x)^n here.
Evaluating at roots of unity solves the count.
animations: Display the text 'Problem: Sum of C(N, k) where 3 divides k' in #FFFFFF.
Show the Generating Function P(x) = (1+x)^N.
Substitute x with 1, ω, and ω^2 in the filter formula.
Visualize (1+ω) as a vector on the complex plane moving to its polar form.
Highlight the final simplified formula for the sum in #FF00FF (Magenta).

storyboard.title: Summary and Conclusion
lecture_lines: First, build your generating function.
Evaluate at roots of unity and average.
Complex geometry simplifies hard counting problems.
animations: Draw a horizontal flowchart: Sequence -> Polynomial -> Unit Circle -> Sum.
Display the text 'Discrete counting meets complex geometry' in #FFFFFF.
Scale up the 'Sum' result and flash it in #FFFF00 to conclude.
